claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 has a high-temperature BCC state.
Chemical short-range order develops in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure.
Differential atomic stresses drive the development of chemical short-range order.
Cr atoms have negative local atomic stress, whereas Co, Fe, Ni, and Al have positive local atomic stresses.
The interplay of negative Cr stress and positive stresses on the other elements creates local compositional fluctuations.
Stress-driven short-range order leads to nucleation of additional phases from the high-temperature BCC state.
Slower cooling permits formation of Cr-rich clusters, whereas faster cooling hinders their formation.
Cr atoms segregate into clusters because of their negative atomic stress.
Cr-rich segregation establishes localized chemical short-range order.
Localized short-range order alters nucleation kinetics and promotes secondary phases such as FCC or intermetallic phases relative to a metastable BCC baseline.
Cooling rate can change the number or identity of phases formed in a multicomponent Cr-containing alloy.
Slow cooling or subsequent annealing of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 will produce additional phases relative to rapid quenching.
Slow-cooled or annealed Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 will contain detectable Cr-rich clusters.
Rapid quenching suppresses atomic diffusion and the establishment of chemical short-range order.
Rapidly quenched Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 will predominantly retain a single-phase BCC structure.
Rapidly quenched Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 will retain a uniform elemental distribution with little to no short-range order.
The proposed mechanism requires thermal paths with sufficient atomic mobility, such as slow cooling or moderate-temperature annealing below the BCC stability range.
The mechanism will be diminished at nanoscale grain sizes because diffusion is constrained.
The mechanism may not apply when Cr concentration or Cr stress characteristics differ significantly.
